name: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy
populations: people with a Haglund prominence or heel spur
summary: Pain, swelling and stiffness at the Achilles insertion on the back of the heel, from tensile and compressive overload against the calcaneus, often with a bursa or spur. End-range dorsiflexion loading aggravates it.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Slow: months of loading, with about two-thirds satisfied at 4 months in a pilot of modified training; surgery only after failed conservative care

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based graded return after a loading phase that avoids end-range dorsiflexion at first

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Tenderness within the distal 2 cm of the tendon at the heel, with pain on dorsiflexion and heel compression

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Lateral weight-bearing radiograph for a spur, calcification or Haglund prominence; ultrasound or MRI for tendon and bursa. Findings track symptoms poorly

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Middle-aged and older adults: mean age 53 in a loading pilot and 59 in a biomechanics study

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: About 6% of people report Achilles pain in their lifetime, and roughly one-third of that is insertional

overview:
Insertional Achilles tendinopathy (IAT) is pain, thickening and degeneration of the Achilles tendon within about 2 cm of its attachment to the calcaneus. It often occurs with a retrocalcaneal bursitis, an enthesophyte (spur) or a posterosuperior calcaneal prominence (Haglund deformity) [r1]. About 6% of people report Achilles pain during their lifetime, and roughly one-third of that is insertional [r1]. Patients report pain with activity, stiffness after rest and difficulty with shoes that press on the back of the heel [r1].

IAT behaves differently from mid-portion tendinopathy. The insertion is loaded in compression as well as tension, and end-range ankle dorsiflexion increases both [r1,r2]. Traditional eccentric heel drops below a step, which suit mid-portion disease, satisfied only 28% to 33% of people with IAT. A modified program that avoids dorsiflexion past neutral and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) have the best, though limited, support [r1,r3,r4].

epidemiology.text: About 6% of the general population reports Achilles tendon pain during their lifetime, and roughly one-third of those people have IAT [r1]. The loading and shockwave trials enrolled adults in mid-to-late life with long symptom duration: mean age 53 and mean pain duration of 26 months in the modified-loading pilot [r3], and mean age 59 in a biomechanics study [r5]. Good population incidence data specific to IAT were not found in the sources reviewed.

intrinsic: Larger heel spurs: spurs were longer on the symptomatic side (12.9 mm) than the asymptomatic side (8.9 mm) or in controls (3.5 mm), although spurs were common on the symptomatic (65%) and asymptomatic (55%) sides [r1]
Altered ankle mechanics: greater end-range dorsiflexion, less plantarflexion and lower peak plantarflexor power on stair ascent (cross-sectional; cause or effect is not established) [r5]
Haglund deformity may compress the tendon and retrocalcaneal bursa in theory, but calcaneal shape angles were not associated with IAT in recent studies [r1]
Gastrocnemius contracture should be tested for, although non-weight-bearing dorsiflexion range did not differ from controls in one study [r1,r5]
Inflammatory disease such as ankylosing spondylitis, in which the entheses are the primary lesion [r6]
extrinsic: Repetitive loading with end-range dorsiflexion, such as hills, stairs and deep heel-drop exercises (mechanistic plausibility) [r1,r2]
Footwear with a rigid heel counter that presses on the posterior heel (patients report shoe sensitivity) [r1]
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics, linked with Achilles tendinopathy and rupture [r7]
Corticosteroid injection around the heel, which has been linked with rupture [r8]

mechanism.summary: IAT results from combined tensile and compressive overload at the insertion. As the calf pulls, the superficial fibres take high axial tensile strain. As the ankle dorsiflexes, the posterosuperior calcaneus presses into the deep fibres and the retrocalcaneal bursa, causing high transverse compressive strain [r1]. Running loads the Achilles 4 to 6 times body weight [r1]. Compression is thought to drive fibrocartilaginous change and proteoglycan build-up in the tendon [r2].
sequence: Repeated running, hill work, stair climbing or calf loading brings the ankle repeatedly toward end-range dorsiflexion.
The calf pulls on the tendon, so the superficial fibres see high tensile strain [r1].
In dorsiflexion the tendon wraps over the posterosuperior calcaneal prominence, which presses on the deep fibres and squeezes the retrocalcaneal bursa [r1,r2].
When the combined load exceeds capacity, the insertion becomes reactive, then disorganised with collagen loss, fatty infiltration and capillary proliferation [r1].
The retrocalcaneal bursa becomes inflamed and tender, and the enthesis may develop a spur or calcification [r1].
The tendon thickens and the back of the heel becomes swollen, stiff after rest and painful in shoes.
Pain changes mechanics: patients used more end-range dorsiflexion and less plantarflexor power on stairs, which can sustain the problem [r5].

variants.name: Haglund deformity with retrocalcaneal bursitis
variants.description: A prominent posterosuperior calcaneus that may compress the tendon and bursa; its causal role is not clearly supported by shape measurements [r1].

variants.name: Calcific insertional tendinopathy
variants.description: Intratendinous calcification or an enthesophyte at the insertion. Spurs are common even without symptoms, but longer spurs were seen on the symptomatic side [r1]. ESWT may be less effective with enthesophytes [r1,r9].

variants.name: Isolated retrocalcaneal bursitis
variants.description: Tenderness anterior to the tendon, with swelling on both sides above the heel; may coexist with IAT [r1].

variants.name: Inflammatory enthesitis
variants.description: In ankylosing spondylitis and related disease the enthesis is the primary lesion, and Achilles enthesitis or retrocalcaneal bursitis can be found, sometimes only on ultrasound [r6].

variants.name: Combined insertional and mid-portion disease
variants.description: Both regions can be involved; assess and load the whole tendon (clinical observation; not quantified in the sources reviewed).

anatomy.text: The Achilles inserts on the posterior calcaneal tuberosity about 2 cm distal to the posterosuperior calcaneal prominence. At this point the tendon is about 5–6 mm thick (anteroposterior) and has medial and lateral projections that form a crescent to spread stress. As the tendon descends it twists, so gastrocnemius fibres insert posterolaterally and soleus fibres anteromedially. A retrocalcaneal bursa lies between the tendon and the calcaneus, and a subcutaneous bursa lies behind the tendon. The insertion is supplied mainly by an arterial plexus on the calcaneus. The sural nerve lies close to the tendon and is relevant to the differential diagnosis and to surgery [r1].

structures.name: Achilles tendon insertion (enthesis)
structures.role: Anchors the triceps surae to the calcaneus; superficial fibres take tension and deep fibres take compression in dorsiflexion [r1]

structures.name: Retrocalcaneal bursa
structures.role: Reduces friction between the anterior tendon and the posterosuperior calcaneus [r1]

structures.name: Posterosuperior calcaneal prominence
structures.role: Bony prominence above the insertion; when enlarged (Haglund deformity), it may compress the tendon and bursa [r1]

structures.name: Kager's fat pad
structures.role: Fat pad anterior to the tendon that fills the space between the tendon, bursa and flexor hallucis longus

structures.name: Subcutaneous (superficial) bursa and skin
structures.role: Pad over the posterior heel that can be irritated by shoe pressure [r1]

structures.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus complex
structures.role: Generates the tensile load on the insertion; gastrocnemius contracture is assessed with the Silfverskiöld test [r1]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Degeneration at the Achilles insertion is the hallmark of IAT. The tendon loses parallel collagen structure and fibre integrity, shows fatty infiltration and capillary proliferation, and becomes thicker and abnormal on imaging; a thickness above 6 mm has been used as a diagnostic criterion [r1]. Compressive load adds a distinct mechanism: it is thought to promote areas of fibrocartilaginous metaplasia and proteoglycan accumulation in the tendon [r2]. The continuum model (reactive, disrepair, degenerative) describes the usual progression in load-induced tendinopathy [r10].

Structure and symptoms correlate poorly. Imaging signs of tendinopathy were present in 0% to 35% of asymptomatic tendons, and absent in 0% to 19% of symptomatic tendons. Enthesophytes were nearly as common on the asymptomatic side (55%) as the symptomatic side (65%) [r1].

structures.name: Achilles insertion
structures.effect: Thickening, disorganised collagen, fatty infiltration and capillary proliferation [r1]

structures.name: Retrocalcaneal bursa
structures.effect: Inflammation and effusion from compression between the tendon and calcaneus; bursitis may coexist with IAT [r1]

structures.name: Posterosuperior calcaneus and enthesis
structures.effect: Enthesophytes and intratendinous calcification are common; longer spurs were found on the symptomatic side [r1]

structures.name: Paratenon and subcutaneous tissues
structures.effect: Paratendinitis and local swelling or redness at the back of the heel [r1]

muscles.name: Triceps surae
muscles.effect: Isometric plantarflexor strength and non-weight-bearing dorsiflexion did not differ from controls in one study, but peak plantarflexor power on stairs was lower [r5].

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.effect: Gastrocnemius contracture or tightness should be screened, but the extent to which it contributes to IAT is not established [r1].

muscles.name: Hip and knee musculature
muscles.effect: Load-sharing across the limb matters for stair and hill work; trial evidence that treating the proximal chain changes IAT outcomes was not found.

cellular.description: Tenocyte activation and matrix swelling after a load spike, especially with dorsiflexion exposure; can reverse with load reduction [r10].
Collagen disorganisation, fatty infiltration and capillary proliferation; compressive load adds fibrocartilaginous change [r1,r2].
Retrocalcaneal bursitis and enthesophyte formation. Osteophytes appear to be a normal response to cumulative loading with age and activity, and larger spurs may relate to symptoms [r1].

systems.effect: Painful tendinopathy shows nerve ingrowth, altered mediators and heightened nociceptor sensitivity, and evidence for central sensitisation exists in chronic Achilles tendinopathy, although studies specific to IAT are lacking [r1].
Altered ankle mechanics on stairs (more end-range dorsiflexion, less plantarflexor power) are linked with greater symptom severity [r5].
Ankylosing spondylitis and related disease cause Achilles enthesitis and retrocalcaneal bursitis, sometimes only visible on ultrasound [r6].
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with Achilles tendinopathy and rupture [r7].
Pain limits work and sport and makes footwear difficult [r1].

grading.system: MRI grading (Nicholson and colleagues, 2007, as reported by Chimenti and colleagues) with the tendinopathy continuum for load-based staging [r1,r10]

grades.description: Anteroposterior tendon diameter 6–8 mm with non-uniform degeneration [r1].
grades.prognosis: Least likely to need surgery (13% in the reported series) [r1]

grades.description: Diameter above 8 mm with uniform degeneration of less than 50% of the tendon width [r1].
grades.prognosis: 91% needed surgery in the reported series; treat as higher risk of failing conservative care [r1]

grades.description: Diameter above 8 mm with uniform degeneration of more than 50% of the tendon width [r1].
grades.prognosis: 70% needed surgery in the reported series [r1]

grades.description: Reactive, disrepair and degenerative stages describe load-based pathology and complement pain and function [r10].
grades.prognosis: Early reactive change settles with load adjustment; established degeneration needs long-term loading

timeframes.summary: IAT is usually a long-standing problem: participants in the loading and shockwave trials had symptoms for months to years (mean 26 months in one pilot, and at least 6 months in an RCT) [r3,r4]. The stage durations below are illustrative. Outcomes of conservative care were assessed at about 4 months, and 12-week loading blocks are the usual unit.

healing.description: Tenocyte activation and swelling after a load spike or dorsiflexion exposure [r10]
Collagen disorganisation with possible retrocalcaneal bursitis [r1]

healing.phase: Established degeneration with enthesophyte or calcification
healing.description: Chronic degenerative change; slow response to treatment [r1]
12 weeks of floor-level loading in the pilot protocol [r3]

milestones.label: 12-week modified loading block complete
milestones.note: 3 × 15 repetitions, twice a day, 7 days a week for 12 weeks in the pilot protocol [r3]

milestones.label: Pilot follow-up: 67% satisfied
milestones.note: At a mean of 4 months, 18 of 27 patients were satisfied and back to loading activity (uncontrolled) [r3]

milestones.label: ESWT vs eccentric loading comparison
milestones.note: VISA-A rose from 53 to 80 with ESWT and from 53 to 63 with eccentric loading at 4 months in an RCT of 50 patients [r4]

milestones.label: Surgical review if conservative care has failed
milestones.note: After months of well-delivered conservative care (a clinical range; the sources reviewed do not set a fixed time) [r1]

milestones.label: ESWT effect stable at one year
milestones.note: The favourable results after shockwave therapy were stable at 1 year [r4]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and slow. Return to running and sport follows a loading phase that restores calf capacity without provoking the heel; in trials, satisfaction and return to previous loading activity were assessed at about 4 months [r3,r4]. Plan on months rather than weeks, and longer for calcific or bilateral disease (clinical range).

symptoms: Pain at the back of the heel where the Achilles inserts, worse with activity and often with hills, stairs or squatting
Stiffness after prolonged rest, such as the first steps in the morning [r1]
Pain or rubbing from shoes that press on the back of the heel [r1]
Swelling and sometimes redness over the posterior heel [r1]
Reduced activity and sport participation over months, often bilateral in some people
signs: Tenderness to palpation within the distal 2 cm of the Achilles tendon [r1]
Thickening at the insertion and a visible or palpable posterior heel prominence or swelling [r1]
Tenderness anterior to the tendon on both sides (retrocalcaneal bursitis) [r1]
Pain on passive dorsiflexion or when the heel is squeezed; pain on single-leg heel raise or hopping
Possible gastrocnemius tightness on the Silfverskiöld test; plantarflexor weakness can be hard to interpret because of pain [r1]

subjective: Site of pain: the back of the heel at the insertion, versus the mid-tendon or the plantar heel
Pattern: pain with activity, stiffness after rest, shoe rubbing, and effect of hills, stairs and heel-drop exercises [r1]
Duration, previous treatment and injections, and response to previous exercise (especially heel drops below a step) [r4]
Bilateral symptoms, morning stiffness, other joint, eye, skin or bowel symptoms (inflammatory disease) [r6]
Fluoroquinolone antibiotic or corticosteroid exposure; diabetes; kidney disease [r7,r8]
Footwear, work demands, training load and goals
observation: Swelling, redness or a bump on the back of the heel (Haglund prominence)
Heel posture and foot alignment, gait and stair strategy (more end-range dorsiflexion was found in IAT) [r5]
Skin condition over the heel and shoe wear pattern
palpation: Palpate the insertion and the distal 2 cm of the tendon [r1]
Palpate both sides of the tendon just above the heel for retrocalcaneal bursitis
Palpate the mid-portion to detect combined disease, and the plantar heel to exclude plantar fasciopathy
Check for a gap (rupture) and for the sural nerve course lateral to the tendon [r1]
rangeOfMotion: Weight-bearing lunge and passive dorsiflexion with the knee straight and bent, compared with the other side
Subtalar and first-ray range as part of the kinetic chain screen
strength: Single-leg heel raise: height, repetitions and pain, compared with the other side
Isometric plantarflexion strength; this may be normal in IAT despite altered stair mechanics [r5]
neuro: Sural nerve sensation and Tinel sign lateral to the tendon (differential for lateral heel pain) [r1]
Distal pulses and sensation if diabetes or neuropathy is suspected
functional: Single-leg hop and repeated hop pain response

specialTests.name: Palpation of the distal 2 cm of the tendon and retrocalcaneal region
specialTests.purpose: Locate tenderness to the insertion versus the mid-portion, bursa or plantar fascia
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the Achilles insertion and the distal 2 cm, then the soft tissue on both sides of the tendon above the heel, and compare with the mid-portion.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness within the distal 2 cm of the tendon, with or without tenderness anterior to the tendon (bursitis).

specialTests.name: Silfverskiöld test
specialTests.purpose: Identify gastrocnemius contracture as a contributor
specialTests.procedure: Measure passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended and again with the knee flexed.
specialTests.positive: Dorsiflexion improves with the knee flexed, suggesting gastrocnemius tightness rather than soleus or joint restriction.

specialTests.name: Single-leg heel raise and hop provocation
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce loading pain and measure calf capacity
specialTests.procedure: Repeated single-leg heel raises from the floor and single-leg hops, comparing pain and repetitions with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the insertion, fewer repetitions or lower height than the other side.

specialTests.name: Thompson (calf squeeze) test
specialTests.purpose: Exclude complete rupture before loading or injecting
specialTests.procedure: Patient prone with the feet over the end of the couch. Squeeze the calf and observe the foot.
specialTests.positive: No plantarflexion on squeeze suggests rupture.

outcomeMeasures.name: VISA-A questionnaire
outcomeMeasures.use: Eight-item severity score (pain, function, sport; 0–100) validated in Achilles tendinopathy and used as the outcome in the IAT shockwave trial [r13,r4]. It is not designed to be diagnostic [r13]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain during Achilles-loading activity (VAS or NPRS)
outcomeMeasures.use: Used to monitor response; the pilot reported VAS 69.9 falling to 21 in satisfied patients [r3]

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient satisfaction and return to previous loading activity
outcomeMeasures.use: Used as a main outcome in IAT studies [r3,r4]

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg heel-rise capacity and stair-ascent performance
outcomeMeasures.use: Calf capacity and stair mechanics, in which IAT patients differed from controls [r5]

imaging.indication: Posterior heel pain with a suspected spur, calcification or Haglund prominence, or before surgery
imaging.findings: Enthesophyte, intratendinous calcification, posterosuperior prominence and Kager's triangle changes suggesting bursitis; spurs are common in people without symptoms [r1]

imaging.indication: Uncertain diagnosis, suspected tear or bursitis, or failed conservative care
imaging.findings: Tendon thickening (a thickness over 6 mm has been used as a criterion), low echogenicity, neovascularisation, retrocalcaneal bursitis [r1]
Tendon thickness and degeneration (Nicholson grades I–III), bursitis and bone marrow change [r1]. Imaging signs and symptoms correlate poorly [r1]

differentials.name: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and thickening 2–6 cm above the heel, with a positive arc sign, rather than within the distal 2 cm at the insertion [r1].

differentials.name: Achilles partial tear or rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden pop, weak push-off, palpable gap and positive Thompson test, often after injection or fluoroquinolone use [r8,r11].

differentials.name: Retrocalcaneal bursitis and Haglund deformity
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness anterior to the tendon on both sides above the heel with a posterosuperior prominence. It often coexists with IAT and may not be separable clinically [r1].

differentials.name: Calcaneal apophysitis (Sever's disease)
differentials.distinguishing: Heel pain in an active child or adolescent with tenderness at the growth plate, not a degenerative Achilles insertion.

differentials.name: Plantar fasciopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Plantar medial heel pain, worse on the first steps in the morning, with tenderness at the plantar fascia origin rather than the posterior heel.

differentials.name: Posterior ankle impingement
differentials.distinguishing: Deep posterior ankle pain on forced plantarflexion, without tendon thickening at the insertion.

differentials.name: Sural nerve irritation or neuroma
differentials.distinguishing: Burning or tingling along the lateral heel with a positive Tinel sign over the nerve near the lateral tendon border [r1].

differentials.name: Spondyloarthropathy enthesitis
differentials.distinguishing: Bilateral heel pain with inflammatory back or joint features and morning stiffness; ultrasound may show enthesitis or bursitis [r6].

redFlags: Sudden pop, loss of push-off, a palpable gap or a positive Thompson test: suspect Achilles rupture. Protect the ankle and arrange urgent orthopaedic review [r11].

Recent corticosteroid injection near the tendon or retrocalcaneal bursa, especially with new sudden pain or weakness: avoid heavy loading and arrange urgent assessment because rupture risk has been described [r8].
Current or recent fluoroquinolone antibiotic use with new Achilles pain: advise the patient to contact the prescriber the same day and avoid heavy loading until the drug is reviewed [r7].
Bilateral heel pain with morning stiffness, other joint pain, back pain, psoriasis, bowel or eye symptoms: suspect inflammatory arthritis or spondyloarthropathy and refer for medical review [r6].
Hot, red, swollen heel, fever, night pain or an open wound over the heel (especially in diabetes): suspect infection of the bursa or calcaneus and arrange urgent medical review.
Calf pain, swelling or warmth: consider deep vein thrombosis and arrange same-day medical assessment.
Persistent severe heel pain after trauma or sudden increase in running, with bony tenderness or pain on squeezing the heel: consider calcaneal stress fracture and arrange imaging.

management.principles: Treat IAT as a load-capacity problem in which compression is a major driver. The core is education, a shift in load away from end-range dorsiflexion, and progressive calf loading that stays within a restricted dorsiflexion range, which has the best support among the loading approaches [r1,r3]. Add ESWT if progress stalls, and consider surgery only after failed conservative care [r1,r9]. The evidence base is thin: most data are from small case series and a few RCTs, and a systematic review of 14 trials could not name a best surgical technique [r9]. Clinical practice also draws on trials in mid-portion disease, which may not transfer [r14].

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection into or around the tendon
medical.description: Largely out of favour for tendinopathy at any site, with particular concern around the Achilles for further degeneration and tear. Isolated retrocalcaneal bursitis might be considered only with great care to avoid the tendon, because a cadaver and case study showed a connection between the bursa and the anterior Achilles fibres [r1,r8].

medical.name: Other injections (PRP, polidocanol, high-volume saline, prolotherapy)
medical.description: The review found insufficient high-quality evidence in IAT to support routine use, and several studies were not specific to IAT. If used at all, it should be specialist-led after loading and ESWT have failed [r1]. The large sham-controlled trial of PRP was in mid-portion disease and was negative [r1].

medical.name: Simple analgesia, short-course NSAIDs and ice
medical.description: May help when inflammation is prominent, such as retrocalcaneal bursitis or paratendinitis. Further research is needed [r1].

medical.name: Review of fluoroquinolone antibiotic use
medical.description: Management of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy includes stopping the drug [r7].

medical.name: Surgical debridement, decompression and calcaneal exostectomy (with or without bursectomy)
medical.description: For patients who fail conservative care. Open debridement and decompression is supported by many studies reporting good function and satisfaction (generally above 87%), but complications ranged from 6% to over 30%, mainly wound problems, painful scar and sural nerve injury [r1]. In a systematic review, five surgical techniques all had good satisfaction (average 89%), but the best technique could not be named [r9].

medical.name: FHL transfer, gastrocnemius recession and endoscopic procedures
medical.description: The review found insufficient evidence to recommend routine use. Flexor hallucis longus transfer did not improve pain or function in a randomised trial of 39 older patients, though it improved plantarflexor strength. Isolated gastrocnemius recession had conflicting low-level evidence [r1].

physio.name: Education and load management
physio.description: Explain that compression and end-range dorsiflexion aggravate the insertion. Modify hills, stairs, deep squats and heel drops below a step, while keeping the patient active. This is a mechanistic approach, supported by the load patterns described in IAT rather than by trials of the education itself [r1,r2].

physio.name: Eccentric or slow loading restricted to floor level (no dorsiflexion past neutral)
physio.description: In a pilot of 27 patients (34 tendons) with a mean pain duration of 26 months, a floor-level eccentric regimen (3 × 15, twice daily, 7 days a week for 12 weeks) left 67% satisfied at a mean of 4 months, with VAS falling from 69.9 to 21 in those who were satisfied [r3]. A review rated limited-range eccentric exercise Grade B and noted that floor-level exercise gave better satisfaction than full-range [r1,r9]. There was no control group in the pilot.

physio.name: Traditional eccentric heel drops below step level as first-line
physio.description: Satisfaction was only 28% to 33% in IAT (Level IV), and about 32% had a good result in the earlier series cited in the pilot, although level I trials show a modest pain reduction of about 1.8 to 2.2 on the VAS [r1,r3]. In an RCT, 28% of the eccentric group were completely recovered or much improved at 4 months compared with 64% after ESWT [r4]. Avoid it as the starting point because dorsiflexion adds compression.

physio.name: Isometric and heavy slow resistance loading within a restricted range
physio.description: Restricting dorsiflexion and using isometric or slow heavy contractions may help to maximise tendon loading, but evidence specific to IAT is lacking [r1]. In mid-portion disease heavy slow resistance and eccentric training gave equally good results at 12 weeks and at 52 weeks, with better compliance for the heavy slow protocol (92% vs 78%) [r14]. This is extrapolated evidence.

physio.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)
physio.description: In an RCT of 50 patients with chronic recalcitrant IAT who had failed at least 3 months of other treatment, VISA-A rose from 53 to 80 with ESWT and from 53 to 63 with eccentric loading at 4 months, and the ESWT result was stable at 1 year [r4]. A systematic review found ESWT superior to wait-and-see and to eccentric training and effective in non-calcified IAT [r9]. There is no standard protocol, treatment can be painful, and effectiveness may be limited with enthesophytes [r1].

physio.name: Heel lift or shoe with a slight heel
physio.description: Biomechanical evidence suggests heel lifts reduce the tendon elongation and compressive strain at the insertion during dorsiflexion tasks. Clinical trial evidence is lacking [r1].

physio.name: Footwear changes to relieve heel counter pressure
physio.description: Soft or open-back shoes can relieve rubbing over the posterior heel. This is practical advice rather than trial-tested [r1].

physio.name: Night splints
physio.description: A review found insufficient evidence for night splints in IAT (Grade I). If a patient can do weight-bearing loading, splints may add nothing [r1].

physio.name: Retraining ankle mechanics on stairs and hills
physio.description: IAT patients used more end-range dorsiflexion and less plantarflexor power on stairs, and these differences were linked with symptom severity; whether retraining helps is untested [r5].

physio.name: Aggressive calf stretching into dorsiflexion
physio.description: Stretching into end-range dorsiflexion increases compressive strain at the insertion and is avoided early. A night splint or gentle stretching with the knee bent are lower-load alternatives [r1,r2].

education: The pain is where the tendon meets the heel bone. It is made worse by being squeezed against the bone, which happens when your foot pulls up toward your shin.
The usual heel-drop exercise off a step can aggravate this problem. We will exercise on flat ground first and build load gradually.
Expect slow progress over months. Many people improve with loading, but some need shockwave therapy and a few need surgery.
A bump or spur on the heel is common and does not mean the tendon is damaged beyond repair. X-rays show spurs in many people without pain.
A heel lift or shoe with a slight heel and a soft heel counter can ease the pressure while you recover.
Do not have a cortisone injection into the tendon area without a specialist discussion. It can weaken the tendon.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and keeps the ankle out of end-range dorsiflexion during the early loading phases, because dorsiflexion increases compression at the insertion [r1,r2]. The program mirrors the pilot of floor-level eccentric loading and the principles of progressive calf loading from mid-portion disease [r3,r14]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not prescriptions from a single trial. A common clinical convention is to accept pain up to about 4–5/10 during exercise provided it settles by the next morning. Plan on months, and review at 12 weeks: if progress has stalled, discuss ESWT [r4].

stages.name: Settle & reduce compression
goals: Reduce load-related heel pain and stiffness
Remove aggravating positions (end-range dorsiflexion, tight shoes)
Keep the calf working in a pain-free range
Teach the load-capacity model and pain monitoring
precautions: Avoid heel drops below a step, deep squats, aggressive calf stretches and steep hills at first [r1]
Avoid steroid injection into or around the tendon [r8]
Keep exercise pain at or below about 4/10 and settled by the next morning (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Isometric standing calf hold on flat ground
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at moderate effort, 1–2 times daily (typical clinical dosage)
exercises.cues: Lift to mid-range only and stay off the end-range of dorsiflexion

exercises.name: Isometric seated calf hold (knee bent)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at moderate effort, 1–2 times daily
exercises.cues: Press through the forefoot and hold steady

exercises.name: Heel lift in the shoe and soft-heel-counter footwear
exercises.dosage: All day while symptoms are irritable
exercises.cues: Reduces dorsiflexion and compression at the insertion [r1]

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels and keep the ribs down

exercises.name: Low-impact conditioning (cycling or pool)
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, 3 times per week, below the pain threshold
exercises.cues: Keep fitness while the heel settles

progressionCriteria: Morning stiffness and pain with daily activity improving
Isometric holds completed without a next-day increase in pain
Rupture excluded and no systemic red flags
Walking comfortable in footwear with a heel lift

stages.name: Floor-level strength (no dorsiflexion)
goals: Build calf capacity without end-range dorsiflexion
Restore single-leg heel raise capacity from the floor
precautions: Lower the heel only to a level, flat-foot (neutral) position, never below it [r3]
Increase load only when next-morning pain is stable
Stop and review if pain at the insertion rises above about 5/10 or lingers into the next day (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Floor-level heel lowering (eccentric, no dorsiflexion)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 15, once or twice daily; the pilot used twice daily, 7 days a week for 12 weeks [r3]
exercises.cues: Rise on both feet, lower slowly on the painful leg, stop at flat foot

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise from the floor (heavy, slow)
exercises.dosage: 3–4 × 6–15, 3 s up and 3 s down, 3 times per week; add load as it becomes easy (typical clinical protocol)
exercises.cues: Full range from flat foot up, no dropping below flat

exercises.name: Seated calf raise with load (soleus)
exercises.cues: Use a load on the thighs

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hips with a long spine

exercises.name: Low step-up
exercises.cues: Use a low box and avoid dropping the heel below it

progressionCriteria: Single-leg floor-level calf raises with load, no more than mild next-day symptoms
Pain during activity usually 3/10 or less
Reassess at 12 weeks; if no progress, discuss ESWT [r4]

stages.name: Graded range, power & plyometrics
goals: Reintroduce small amounts of dorsiflexion range only if tolerated
precautions: Add dorsiflexion range gradually (for example a thin step) and only if the next-day response is stable
Stop and re-plan if the heel flares

exercises.name: Calf raise from a thin step (small dorsiflexion range)
exercises.cues: Lower only a small amount below flat foot, if tolerated

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place
exercises.cues: Land softly and keep the heel quiet

progressionCriteria: No increase in heel pain or morning stiffness after plyometrics
Single-leg heel-rise capacity near the other side (clinical convention)

stages.name: Return to running & sport
goals: Graded return to running, hills and sport-specific tasks
precautions: Increase volume before intensity, and add hills late because they increase dorsiflexion
Allow rest days between early running sessions
Keep a heel lift or suitable footwear if it helps

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Alternate short jog and walk intervals on non-consecutive days and build jog time as pain allows (typical clinical protocol)
exercises.cues: Monitor pain during and the next morning

exercises.name: Continuous running with gradual weekly progression
exercises.dosage: Increase total volume by modest steps weekly, then add speed, then hills
exercises.cues: Short, quick steps and a quiet heel

exercises.name: Sport-specific jumping and change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions per week, from controlled to unplanned

exercises.name: Heavy calf strength maintenance
exercises.cues: Keep this in the program long term

progressionCriteria: Completes the running program without a next-day increase in heel pain or stiffness
Single-leg heel-rise endurance and hop tests near symmetrical (clinical convention)
Tolerates sport training at full intensity for a week
Understands pain monitoring and load management [r15]

criteria: Heel pain with daily activity and load tests minimal, and no next-day flare after running or jumping (clinical convention)
Single-leg heel-rise endurance and hop tests near symmetrical with the other side (clinical convention)
Completed a graded running and jumping program without a flare [r15]
VISA-A score improving toward healthy-control levels (mean above 96 in the original validation study) [r13]
Footwear and load plan agreed, with continued calf strength work
tests: Single-leg heel-rise endurance or work, compared with the other side
Pain response to loading and the next morning

prognosis: IAT is often persistent. In a pilot of modified floor-level loading, 67% of 27 patients were satisfied at a mean of 4 months, and 9 patients were not satisfied despite lower pain scores [r3]. In an RCT of 50 patients with chronic recalcitrant IAT, 64% in the ESWT group and 28% in the eccentric group were recovered or much improved at 4 months, and the ESWT results were stable at 1 year [r4]. After surgery, satisfaction is generally above 87%, but complications ranged from 6% to over 30% [r1]. On MRI, 13% of grade I, 91% of grade II and 70% of grade III tendons needed surgery in one reported series, so imaging grade may help to predict surgical need [r1].
prevention: No prevention trials specific to IAT were found. Build running and hill volume gradually and avoid repeated end-range dorsiflexion overload (mechanistic reasoning) [r1,r2].
Choose footwear that does not press on the posterior heel, and use a heel lift if symptoms start (practical advice) [r1].
Maintain calf strength and capacity with regular heavy calf work (clinical practice).
Review fluoroquinolone antibiotic use in people with Achilles symptoms and avoid corticosteroid injections near the tendon [r7,r8].
Screen for inflammatory arthritis in people with bilateral or recurrent heel pain [r6].
clinicalPearls: Insertional pain lies within about 2 cm of the heel. Mid-portion tendinopathy is higher, and the loading advice differs [r1].
Do not default to the Alfredson heel-drop. Full-range eccentric exercise satisfied only 28–33% of people with IAT, whereas floor-level loading satisfied 67% in a pilot (uncontrolled) [r1,r3].
Spurs and calcification are common and do not prove the diagnosis. Spurs were present on the asymptomatic side in 55%, though longer spurs were seen on the symptomatic side [r1].
Imaging tracks symptoms poorly (signs in up to 35% of asymptomatic tendons). Use it to plan surgery or exclude other pathology, not to name the cause [r1].
ESWT outperformed eccentric loading at 4 months in the only RCT, but may be less helpful with a calcified enthesis or a large spur [r4,r1,r9].
Ask about injections and antibiotics, and consider spondyloarthropathy when pain is bilateral or has inflammatory features [r8,r7,r6].

forces.label: Tendon pressed onto the heel bone

captions.text: A runner adds hills and stairs to training. Every stride loads the Achilles insertion at the heel.
In stance the ankle dorsiflexes, and the calf pulls on the tendon: tension on the surface fibres.
At the same time the tendon wraps over the back of the heel bone, so its deep fibres are squeezed.
Dorsiflexion adds compression to tension, so the insertion takes a different load from the mid-tendon.
When this combined load exceeds capacity, the insertion becomes painful over weeks.
There is no single injury moment: pain and stiffness at the back of the heel build gradually.
Zooming into the right heel and the Achilles insertion, viewed from behind.

actions.label: Heel bone presses on the tendon

captions.text: The Achilles inserts on the back of the heel bone, with a bursa tucked in front of it.
The calf pulls the tendon up, while the bony prominence of the heel pushes against it.
In dorsiflexion the deep fibres and the retrocalcaneal bursa are compressed against the heel bone.
The bursa becomes irritated and inflamed.
The tendon insertion thickens and degenerates; it does not tear.
Calcification or a spur may form. These are common even without pain, so their size matters more than their presence.
Scans show these changes poorly matched to symptoms, so diagnosis stays clinical.
Healthy tendon: tightly packed, aligned type I collagen with a few resident tenocytes.
Reactive: under tension and compression, tenocytes activate and the matrix swells.
Disrepair: collagen becomes disorganised and new vessels appear.
Degenerative: areas of cell death and disorganised matrix remain, with limited capacity to reverse.
Progressive loading that avoids end-range dorsiflexion builds capacity as the tendon adapts.
